name: Hair volume / quiff for height

lead: Styling hair upward, as in a quiff or pompadour, adds visible height at the top of the head and a longer head-to-body line, which users say makes them look taller. The change shows immediately.

A quiff has longer hair at the front combed up and back, with shorter sides; it combines elements of the 1950s pompadour and flattop and was a staple of the British Teddy Boy movement. No studies were found on whether upswept hair changes perceived height, and forum discussion centres on keeping fine or straight hair voluminous.

paras: Hair is lifted at the front using styling products, blow drying or overnight techniques, with shorter sides to keep the focus on the top. Fine hair usually needs volume products and a good cut to hold the shape.
Low risk. Styling products and heat can affect hair condition. No studies on perceived-height effects were found.

angle.text: Styling hair upward in a quiff or pompadour adds visible height on top and a longer vertical line. The change is visible immediately; perceived-height effects on others have not been studied.

lead: Styling hair upward, as in a quiff or pompadour, is discussed in looksmaxxing circles as a way to add apparent height and a longer head-to-body line. A quiff has longer hair at the front combed up and back, with shorter sides.[1][2]

The quiff combines elements of the 1950s pompadour and flattop and was a staple of the British Teddy Boy movement, returning in the 1980s and 1990s.[2] The pompadour, a large volume of hair swept up from the forehead, was popularised in the 1950s by Elvis Presley and James Dean.[3]
No studies were found on whether upswept hair changes perceived height. Forum discussion centres on how to keep fine or straight hair voluminous.

paras: The modern quiff leaves hair longer at the front tapering toward trimmed sides and back.[2] The Japanese Regent is a similar style.[2] The etymology of quiff is uncertain, with French coiffe and Dutch kuif proposed.[2][1]

Adding height to hair began at the French court in the 1680s for women.[3] The men's quiff emerged in post-war Britain as a reaction to short military cuts and spread with rock and roll.[1][2] Pomade and Brylcreem helped hold the shape.[1]

Users on looksmax.org share methods to boost volume in thin or straight hair, such as tying long hair up overnight and blow drying.[4] Responders in the same thread report that such methods work for them while others question the reasoning.[4]

lore.intro: Hair volume is discussed on forums mainly as a styling challenge for fine hair, sometimes tied to looking taller.[4]

claims.claim: Tying hair up overnight gives 'volume' without product.
Upswept hair makes you look taller.
